251.quote_or_event: “He eats crisp goats’ meat, his belly grows, and his veins swell with blood--but he gains nothing but life in hell, just as the ram is only fed to be killed for the sake of a guest.”
251.explanation: In the parable of the ram, the meat-eater who fattens his body on other creatures' flesh is compared to a ram fattened for slaughter: all his feeding only readies him for hell.
251.tie_back: Valluvar asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can be ruled by compassion; the Uttaradhyayana uses the same image of a body swelling on another creature's meat and calls it ripening for hell.
251._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the shared image of fattening one's own flesh on another's is a close match, though the Sutra stresses the karmic outcome rather than the loss of compassion.

252.quote_or_event: “In compassion to all beings, the seers, the Gñâtriputras, avoid what is sinful; afraid of it, they abstain from food especially prepared for them.”
252.explanation: Answering Buddhists who defend eating meat prepared for monks, Ardraka says the followers of Mahavira refuse such food because of their compassion for all beings.
252.tie_back: Valluvar says flesh-eaters cannot enjoy the possession of compassion; Ardraka presents refusing meat-dishes as the natural working of compassion for all beings.
252._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's italic transliteration marks removed from 'Gñâtriputras'); it shares the link between compassion and refusing meat but lacks the kural's comparison with wealth that is not guarded.

253.quote_or_event: “A man who always feeds two thousand worthy monks, does not control himself, and will be blamed in this world like a man with bloody hands. They kill a fattened sheep, and prepare food for the sake of a particular person; they season the meat with salt and oil, and dress it with pepper.”
253.explanation: Ardraka says that a patron who has a sheep killed and its meat seasoned to feed monks stands, for all his piety, like a man with bloody hands.
253.tie_back: Valluvar compares the mind of one who relishes flesh to the heart of one who holds a weapon; Ardraka likewise puts the provider of a meat feast alongside a man with blood on his hands.
253._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the bloody-hands image is close to the kural's weapon-holder, but it is aimed at the patron who supplies the meat, and it is not a claim about how relishing flesh shapes the mind.

254.quote_or_event: “A wise man should study them with all means of philosophical research. All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything.”
254.explanation: The Sutrakritanga sums up the whole path in one rule: because every being hates pain, wisdom comes down to not killing anything.
254.tie_back: Valluvar answers 'what is compassion?' with 'not killing'; the Sutrakritanga answers 'what is wisdom?' with the same reply.
254.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.9-10 (also at I.1.4.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
254._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on non-killing as the core definition, though this verse does not take up the kural's further point that eating the flesh is also wrong.

255.quote_or_event: “You like meat minced or roasted; I have been made to eat, ever so many times, poisoned meat, and red-hot to boot.” … “Always frightened, trembling, distressed, and suffering, I have experienced the most exquisite pain and misery.”
255.explanation: Prince Mrigaputra recalls his past lives in hell for his parents, setting the meat they enjoy beside the poisoned, red-hot meat he was forced to eat there.
255.tie_back: Valluvar warns that hell will swallow the flesh-eater and not let him go; Mrigaputra's account of the hells pairs the taste for meat with its endless repayment there.
255._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the verse sets a liking for meat against torment in hell, but it does not explicitly say that eating meat is the cause, and the kural's first line (life depends on not eating flesh) has no parallel here.

256.quote_or_event: “A true monk should not accept such food and drink as has been especially prepared for him along with slaughter of living beings.” … “Those who praise the gift, are accessory to the killing of beings.”
256.explanation: The Sutrakritanga holds that whoever consumes food or approves of gifts that involve killing shares in the guilt of the killing.
256.tie_back: Valluvar answers the buyer who says 'I did not kill' by showing that demand creates the killing; Jain teaching likewise makes the one who accepts or praises slaughtered food an accessory to the slaughter.
256.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.14, I.11.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
256._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the principle of complicity through consumption or approval, but it addresses monks' alms and gifts rather than the market link between eating and selling meat.

257.quote_or_event: “all beings, those with two, three, four senses, plants, those with five senses, and the rest of creation, (experience) individually pleasure or displeasure, pain, great terror, and unhappiness.” … “some kill (them) for the sake of their flesh, some kill them for the sake of their blood”
257.explanation: The Acaranga first insists that every creature feels pain and terror, then lists the killing of animals for their flesh and blood among the sinful acts a wise man must give up.
257.tie_back: Valluvar says that if people truly saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it; the Acaranga likewise asks the reader to see the pain and terror behind every piece of flesh taken.
257.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.6.2, I.1.6.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
257._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong thematic fit (seeing the suffering behind meat), though it lacks the kural's striking image of flesh as a wound.

258.quote_or_event: “You are irreligious, unworthy men, devoted to foolish pleasures, who say that partaking heartily of this meat you are not soiled by sin. All who partake of such food, commit sins in their ignorance; but the wise do nothing of the kind.”
258.explanation: Ardraka rejects the claim that one can eat meat without moral stain, saying meat-eating comes from ignorance and the wise do not do it.
258.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose vision is free of delusion will not eat lifeless flesh; Ardraka likewise contrasts the ignorance of meat-eaters with the wise, who abstain.
258._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close on wisdom versus ignorance in abstaining from meat, though it is set in a polemic against Buddhist monks and lacks the kural's wordplay on separation from fault and from life.

259.quote_or_event: “You (use) Kusa-grass, sacrificial poles, straw and wood, you touch water in the evening and in the morning; thereby you injure living beings, and in your ignorance you commit sins again and again.” … “Penance is my fire; life my fireplace; right exertion is my sacrificial ladle; the body the dried cowdung; Karman is my fuel; self-control, right exertion, and tranquillity are the oblations, praised by the sages, which I offer.”
259.explanation: The outcaste-born monk Harikesa tells Brahmin sacrificers that their fire rites injure living beings, and redefines true sacrifice as inner discipline whose first rule is 'doing no injury to living beings' (12.41).
259.tie_back: Valluvar ranks not killing a single creature above a thousand fire sacrifices; Harikesa likewise sets non-injury and inner penance above, and against, the Vedic fire offering.
259._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's italic markup removed from 'Kusa'); a strong fit on ethical restraint over ritual sacrifice, though the Sutra does not make the kural's numerical comparison.

260.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Dasavaikalika Sutra, placed in the Saman Suttam's Dharmasutra, calls dharma the highest good, names its essence as non-violence (ahimsa), self-control (samyama) and penance (tapas), and says that even the gods bow down to one whose mind is always set on dharma.
260.explanation: Jain tradition holds that one whose life is grounded in non-violence wins the reverence even of the gods.
260.tie_back: Valluvar says all living beings will join their palms in worship of the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; the Dasavaikalika says the gods themselves bow to the one whose dharma is rooted in ahimsa.
260.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1, as Saman Suttam v. 82 (Dharmasutra)
260._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. I confirmed the Prakrit and the verse number 82 on a jainworld.com Saman Suttam page (Spanish rendering), but I could not load an English page to check exact wording. A close fit, though in it the gods, not all living beings, offer the homage.
